subject: music
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What percentage of the total Edexcel GCSE Music (1MU0) qualification is Component 2: Composing worth?
questions.explain: Component 2 (Composing) carries 30% of the overall GCSE Music mark.

questions.q: How many compositions must a candidate submit for Component 2?
questions.explain: Candidates submit two compositions: one free composition and one composition to a brief.

questions.q: What is the total number of marks available for Component 2: Composing?
questions.explain: The two compositions are each worth 30 marks, giving 60 marks in total.

questions.q: How many marks is each individual composition worth in Component 2?
questions.explain: Each of the two compositions is marked out of 30, totalling 60 marks.

questions.q: What is the minimum combined playing time required across both compositions in Component 2?
questions.explain: The two compositions together must last a minimum of three minutes.

questions.q: Who sets the brief used for the 'composition to a brief'?
options: An external composer chosen by the school
questions.explain: For this composition, candidates choose from a set of briefs released by Pearson.

questions.q: Who sets the brief for the 'free composition'?
questions.explain: In the free composition the candidate devises their own brief, with freedom of style and instrumentation.

questions.q: The Pearson-set briefs for the composition to a brief are each linked to what?
questions.explain: Each released brief connects to one of the four areas of study from the specification.

questions.q: Which of the following is a musical element that composers control?
questions.explain: Texture is a musical element; the others are forms or terms rather than elements.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the musical element of 'texture'?
options: The way different layers of sound combine
The overall speed of the music
The tone colour of an instrument
The pattern of strong and weak beats
questions.explain: Texture concerns how many musical layers sound together and how they relate, e.g. monophonic or homophonic.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the element of 'timbre'?
options: The tone colour or quality of a sound
The key the music is in
questions.explain: Timbre refers to the distinctive tone colour that distinguishes one sound source from another.

questions.q: A composer describes their piece as being in a minor key that shifts to major. Which musical element are they manipulating?
questions.explain: Tonality concerns whether music is major, minor or otherwise, and changes between them.

questions.q: What is the main difference between the free composition and the composition to a brief?
options: The free composition lets the candidate set their own brief, while the other uses a Pearson-set brief
The free composition is worth more marks
The free composition must be for voice only
The free composition does not need a recording
questions.explain: The free composition gives creative freedom over the brief; the other must respond to a Pearson-set brief.

questions.q: Why is 'musical coherence' assessed in each composition?
options: To reward ideas that are developed and connected into a unified whole
To reward the loudest possible dynamics
To reward using the greatest number of instruments
To reward the longest possible piece
questions.explain: Coherence rewards a piece whose ideas are shaped and linked so it holds together convincingly.

questions.q: How is each finished composition normally submitted for assessment?
options: As an audio recording together with a score or written account
As a live performance in the exam hall
As a set of song lyrics
questions.explain: Compositions are submitted as a recording supported by a score or written account of the music.

questions.q: Adding a countermelody above the main tune changes which musical element most directly?
questions.explain: Introducing an extra melodic layer thickens the texture of the music.

questions.q: A candidate wants complete freedom over the style, mood and instrumentation of their piece. Which composition should they use for this?
options: Both must follow the same fixed style
questions.explain: The free composition allows the candidate to choose the style and instrumentation themselves.

questions.q: A brief asks for a piece for a solo instrument in a Baroque or Classical style. Which area of study does it most clearly relate to?
questions.explain: Baroque and Classical instrumental writing sits within the Instrumental Music 1700-1820 area of study.

questions.q: To create a build-up towards a climax, a candidate adds a gradual increase in volume and sharper accents. Which two musical elements are they using?
questions.explain: A crescendo controls dynamics, while accents control articulation.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Music (1MU0) specification; Component 2: Composing
